newsitem.title: USA: INTERVIEW-SoCalEd can match rate base cuts.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-SoCalEd can match rate base cuts.

text.p: Southern California Edison will match the reductions in its rate base from securitization and asset sales to maintain its financial structure, Treasurer Theodore F. Craver Jr told Reuters.

The utility's previously announced plans to sell 12 generating plants and rate reduction bonds approved by the California legislature will reduce SoCal Edison's assets and rate base, he explained in an interview.
There will need to be an offsetting reduction in liabilities and equity to allow the utility to reduce rates.
Craver said SoCal Edison faces no impediments to this "capital rebalancing" from trust indentures on its debt.
"In our case, we're able to (retire debt) without triggering any kind of early call on outstanding" issues, he said.

The company's planning assumes maintenance of the same capital structure, so any retirement of debt will have to be matched -- on a percentage basis -- by equity distributions. Since the utility's equity is held by Edison International, this will mean dividend payments to the parent company, where Craver also holds the title of Treasurer, he said.
Edison International will probably use the money to fund its stock buy-back program which could well be expanded again in the future, the official said.
He said competing uses of the funds would have to provide a greater return to the company in improved earnings per share to compete with the buy-back program.

The California Public Utilities Commission is holding a workshop next week on the rate reduction bonds, Craver said, pointing out that it "helps to coordinate as much as possible (with the state's other utilities) on the structure" of the bonds.
He expects SoCal Edison to file with the commission in April for permission to issue the bonds.
He said the utility's plans to sell 12 natural gas fired power plants was "on track" toward the goal of selling the "non-must run" plants by January 1, 1998.
These "non-must run" plants were being sold without contracts to purchase facility's power, he noted.
Currently, Craver said, the utility considers six of the twelve plants to be "must run" -- that they is must be kept in operation for local reliability reasons.
However, SoCal Edison was seeking approval for transmission upgrades that would put four of the six into this "non-must run" category.
The utility's "must run" assessment of each plant was subject to confirmation by California's ISO -- independent system operator -- Associate General Counsel Ann Cohen said.
This is not expected before late June or early July, she added.

Craver said this will delay the beginning of the auction process, which the utility had hoped to start May 15. But the sale of the "non-must run" plants was still expected to be completed by year end.
He said over 300 potential buyers and investors attended SoCal Edison's three pre-bid conferences in Los Angeles, Houston and New York this week.
The company was "satisfied (the meetings) met our primary objective" -- to get the word about the auction process out and create excitment about the sale.
((-- New York Newsdesk 212-859-1610))
